# On Mnw: a letter to a colleague

*A letter to a colleague, 31 July 2026 — on the name Mnw, and on the forms that keep failing it.*

Your note said, roughly: surely the marks are a nicety. Permit me to use Mnw to show they are not.

First, the attestation. The attested form is **𓀽**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Mnw**.

Say it aloud as the sources heard it: “MIN” The marks are what carry that sound to a reader who has never heard it spoken.

On the plain form — and I want to be precise, because you pushed on this. The plain form *min* is *not false — it is a fallback*, and the register is exact about what that means. In systems that cannot carry diacritics (legacy databases, older tooling, parts of the address-bar pipeline) the flattened form is the accepted vehicle, and the rulebook names it explicitly as the final rung of the fallback hierarchy: full restoration first, circumflex where attested, macron-only by the academic standard, an attested variant, and only then plain ASCII.

What the fallback status forbids is promotion: *min* may carry the name where marks are impossible, but it may not *represent* the name where marks are possible.  A fallback is a vehicle, never the primary.

One more thing, because it always surprises: the name did not stay home. The Greeks named him Pan without hesitation, and Roman Egypt painted him in both divine dialects at once.  Within Egypt he fused with Horus as ‘Min-Horus the victorious’, with Amun-Ra in the Theban Ramesside theology, and with Osiris in the funerary visitations — a god whose essence, enduring potency, annexed whatever it touched.

And it never stopped working. Min’s harvest festival is the ancestor of every ‘first sheaf’ ceremony documented in the Mediterranean; Herodotus’ Pan-equation is still cited as the founding gesture of comparative mythology.  Coptos, his city, guarded the desert routes whose exploitation made Egypt’s Eastern Desert gold famous.

## The Convention's Own History

Egyptological transliteration exists because hieroglyphs write consonants, not vowels. The characters ꜣ (aleph) and ꜥ (ayin) are consonants — a glottal reed and a pharyngeal grip — and rendering them as vowels does not "simplify" the name, it deletes consonants from it. The conventions in use descend from nineteenth-century decipherment and the standardized Manuel de Codage: ḥ, ḫ, ḏ, ṯ each mark a distinct consonant the Egyptian wrote and a modern reader must not merge. When this register defends them, it defends the principle that a writing system older than the alphabet gets to keep its consonants.

## The Address, Without an Encoding Detour

The canonical form **Mnw** already uses ordinary Latin letters, so the address bar needs no special encoding narrative. The digital temple can preserve the spelling exactly as the scholarly record presents it. That is the practical point here: consistency between the source, the citation, and the public address.

This does not make every romanization equally valid. A wrong letter remains wrong even when it is easy to type. Canonical status still depends on the attested convention, never on convenience or registrar inventory.

Write back when you have checked the sources; they are better company than I am.

*— The Register*

## The Verdict

**Mnw** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *min* is sanctioned as the fallback vehicle and nothing more. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Mnw** stands at [/min/](/min/).

The docket for this ruling: no false forms on the docket; no contested forms attested; the attestation rests on 4 cited sources — Herodotus, Histories 2.46 (the procession and the Pan-equation), Festival reliefs of the Ramesseum and Medinet Habu (the Min procession), Predynastic Min-standard iconography (Scorpion macehead).
